title: Partitioning
subtitle: Single-node table partitioning (Range, List, Hash), Vertical Partitioning, and Partition Pruning for massive tables.
keyTakeaways: Table partitioning splits a large table into smaller physical sub-tables on a single database node while presenting a single unified table view to applications.
Partition Pruning allows the query planner to inspect `WHERE` clauses and read only the matching partition, completely skipping gigabytes of unneeded data.
Dropping an expired month partition via `DROP TABLE` is an instant O(1) operation that generates zero WAL overhead, unlike `DELETE` which causes severe table bloat.

sections.heading: Horizontal Partitioning: Range, List, and Hash
sections.body: Unlike sharding (which distributes data across independent network servers), single-node table partitioning divides a massive table into smaller physical backing tables within the same database engine. When a table grows to hundreds of millions of rows, its B-Tree indexes exceed available RAM, turning every query into a slow random disk seek. Partitioning keeps individual sub-table indexes small enough to fit in the database buffer pool cache.
bullets: Range Partitioning: Partitions by date or numeric range (e.g., one partition per calendar month). Ideal for time-series data, transaction logs, and audit trails.
List Partitioning: Partitions by explicit discrete values (e.g., `country_code IN ('US', 'CA')`). Best for regulatory data residency compliance on a single server.
Hash Partitioning: Partitions by a modulus hash of a key to evenly distribute rows across a fixed number of sub-tables.

Partition Pruning: The database query optimizer detects partition constraints in queries (`WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-01'`) and scans only the October partition, ignoring all other historical partitions.

sections.heading: Vertical Partitioning: Row Splitting and TOAST
sections.body: Vertical partitioning splits a wide table with dozens of columns into separate tables sharing the same primary key, separating frequently accessed hot columns from rarely accessed wide text columns.
bullets: Column Isolation: Moving wide columns (`user_bio TEXT`, `resume_pdf BLOB`) to a separate table (`user_profiles_extended`) allows the primary `users` table to pack ten times more rows per 8 KB database page, dramatically increasing buffer pool cache efficiency.
TOAST in PostgreSQL: Postgres automatically vertical-partitions large fields out-of-line into TOAST (The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique) tables when row size exceeds 2 KB.

tradeOffs.pros: O(1) data lifecycle pruning via `DROP TABLE`; queries benefit from partition pruning; indexes fit into memory.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires automated cron jobs to provision upcoming month partitions; queries without partition keys must scan all sub-tables.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Time-series logging, financial audit records, and analytical event tables.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero partition management overhead; global unique constraints enforced natively by database engine.
tradeOffs.cons: B-Tree indexes eventually exceed RAM; data retention deletes (`DELETE FROM ... WHERE created_at < ...`) saturate WAL and cause table bloat.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Small to medium tables (<10 million rows) with uniform access patterns.

interviewTip: When discussing historical data retention (e.g., storing 5 years of logs but purging data older than 90 days), recommend Range Partitioning: 'Instead of running an expensive DELETE query that causes massive WAL write spikes and table bloat, we range-partition audit logs by month. Purging data older than 90 days is a sub-millisecond `DROP TABLE` operation that instantly reclaims disk space.'
